candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Possible morally sufficient reasons for permitting suffering defeat the claimed logical incompatibility between God and evil.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted rebuttal is delivered in Craig's first-person voice and explicitly addresses Grayling by name.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This move directly contests a necessary premise of the logical problem of evil and assigns its proof burden to the atheist.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Grayling's claim that a powerful and benevolent deity would not permit terrible suffering.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig distinguishes divine obligations from those of a human father, invokes possible overriding reasons, and argues that logical incompatibility remains unproved.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Human cognitive limitations prevent justified probability judgments that God lacks sufficient reasons for observed evil.
candidates.attributionBasis: Craig announces his probabilistic case in the first person and develops it continuously until introducing his second point.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument attacks the evidential inference from apparently gratuitous suffering to God's improbability by challenging human epistemic competence.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The secular inference that the world's observed suffering makes a concerned deity unreasonable or improbable.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig lists limits on human knowledge and uses chaos theory and a branching-life illustration to argue that distant consequences cannot reliably be assessed.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Christian theism makes evil less improbable because suffering may help bring people freely into God's kingdom and eternal life.
candidates.attributionBasis: The same identified Craig speech continues, with an explicit transition to his second probabilistic point and Christian commitments.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies an affirmative theistic explanation for why natural and moral evil could coexist with a divine salvific purpose.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The argument that natural and moral evils make the existence of the Christian God improbable.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig says God's primary purpose is knowledge of himself rather than earthly happiness and treats suffering as a possible means toward freely accepted salvation.

candidates.speaker: A. C. Grayling
candidates.proposition: Theological qualifications repeatedly move the concept of God away from the familiar caring-father model used to motivate belief.
candidates.attributionBasis: Grayling begins after applause, thanks the preceding speaker, identifies himself as the atheist, and answers Craig's father analogy.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move challenges the conceptual stability of the theistic defense and argues that its qualifications undermine ordinary grounds for understanding divine goodness.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's rejection of the human-father analogy and his qualified account of divine power and moral responsibility.

candidates.contextSummary: Grayling argues that attempts to reason from a loving creator continually encounter revised divine attributes, leaving the proposed moral relationship obscure.

candidates.speaker: A. C. Grayling
candidates.proposition: The distinction between a logically possible world and one feasible for God is insufficiently explained, especially regarding free creatures without natural evil.
candidates.attributionBasis: Grayling explicitly refers to Craig's possible-versus-feasible distinction and develops the objection in one uninterrupted passage.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This attacks the mechanism by which the free-will defense seeks to deny that God could actualize a better world containing free agents.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's claim that logically possible worlds containing free agents and less evil may nevertheless be infeasible for God.

candidates.contextSummary: Grayling accepts a distinction between possibility and desirability but says he cannot see the asserted difference between logical possibility and divine feasibility.

candidates.speaker: A. C. Grayling
candidates.proposition: Appealing to unknown morally sufficient reasons for tsunamis and childhood cancer does not make belief in a caring powerful deity reasonable.
candidates.attributionBasis: Grayling names Craig's morally sufficient reasons claim and tests it against the debate's concrete examples of severe suffering.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly addresses the debate's governing question by arguing that unexplained possible goods cannot reconcile traditional divine attributes with the actual world.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's appeal to unknown morally sufficient divine reasons for permitting terrible pain and suffering.

candidates.contextSummary: Grayling argues that merely trusting that drowning or painful cancer serves an unknown good leaves an incoherence between a concerned powerful being and this world.

candidates.speaker: A. C. Grayling
candidates.proposition: Neither expert abandonment of the logical problem nor appeals to human ignorance and Christian doctrine adequately answer the probabilistic problem of evil.
candidates.attributionBasis: Grayling explicitly enumerates and responds to Craig's stated objections to the logical and probabilistic arguments from evil.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This consolidated reply rejects Craig's authority appeal, skeptical-theist reasoning, and Christian framing as support for the coexistence of God and evil.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's claims about philosophical consensus, cognitive limits, Christian doctrine, and the total evidential case.

candidates.contextSummary: Grayling says authority does not refute an argument, ignorance cannot supply unknown justifying goods, and the Gospel portrait of God conflicts with natural evil.

candidates.speaker: A. C. Grayling
candidates.proposition: Ordinary moral knowledge remains reliable enough to assess suffering despite uncertainty about remote consequences and chaotic causal effects.
candidates.attributionBasis: Grayling directly identifies Craig's utilitarian and butterfly-effect argument and answers it with ordinary examples of foreseeable consequences.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument resists skeptical theism by defending the human capacity to make sufficiently dependable moral judgments about harms and benefits.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's contention that unpredictable long-term consequences prevent justified judgments about apparently gratuitous evil.

candidates.contextSummary: Grayling contrasts giving ice cream with kicking an ankle and argues that practical moral understanding is rich enough to bear on the reasonableness question.

candidates.speaker: A. C. Grayling
candidates.proposition: The harsh facts of the world make belief in even a minimally aware and influential supernatural being unreasonable on the total evidence.
candidates.attributionBasis: Grayling identifies the conclusion as his own task and closes the speech immediately before music, applause, and moderator remarks.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is Grayling's culminating application of the world's suffering to the motion, extending the objection from traditional theism to a minimal deity.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's claim that Christian salvation and future fulfillment reconcile divine goodness with suffering in this life.

candidates.contextSummary: Grayling contrasts pastoral assurances with sophisticated qualifications, characterizes future compensation as a blank check, and concludes that the total evidence diminishes reasonableness.

candidates.speaker: A. C. Grayling
candidates.proposition: A world containing free individuals but no natural evil appears logically possible, so the theist must explain why it would be infeasible for God.
candidates.attributionBasis: The alternating dialogue and direct second-person challenge identify Grayling as responding to Craig's renewed account of classical omnipotence.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The challenge targets a crucial gap between logical possibility and divine feasibility in extending the free-will defense to natural rather than moral evil.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's insistence that classical omnipotence excludes only contradictions and that some possible worlds are not feasible.

candidates.contextSummary: Grayling sets aside verbal contradictions such as round squares and asks for a substantive reason why free creatures could not inhabit a world without natural evil.
